steps.text:
INTRODUCTION
Pipelines are a very common way of transporting fluid media, and they have a big impact on many parts of our daily lives. They have many roles, from transporting water, gases, and oils to the circulation of bodily fluids. The sizes of these pipelines vary a lot, from sub-millimeter dimensions in biological systems to industrial ones that measure tens of centimeters. They also have different curvatures, both straight and sharply curved, and many structural variations, from rigid to soft. Their length can be anything from just centimeters to hundreds of meters. Even though pipelines have such a wide range of attributes, they all need one thing in common, which is regular inspections so that they keep functioning properly. For this, several pipeline inspection robots have been developed for different applications.

Many inspection robots have been developed for navigating pipelines, including wheel-type robots, walking-type robots, crawler-type robots, screw-driven type robots and robots with other locomotion mechanisms. These robots usually have rigid structures and are powered by electric motors and gear transmission systems, which makes them good for inspecting pipelines with larger diameters. But these designs have some limitations. For example they are not flexible, and this makes it hard for them to adapt to pipelines of different sizes. Downsizing these robots is also very challenging, especially for millimeter-scale pipelines like the ones found in biological systems. Also, their mechanisms are intricate and need complex assembly structures, which need a lot of maintenance and can also fail if debris gets into their joints. Using soft material can reduce these drawbacks by making the robot completely soft.

  - promising for pipeline inspection

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
INTRODUCTION
Pipelines are a very common way of transporting fluid media, and they have a big impact on many parts of our daily lives. They have many roles, from transporting water, gases, and oils to the circulation of bodily fluids. The sizes of these pipelines vary a lot, from sub-millimeter dimensions in biological systems to industrial ones that measure tens of centimeters. They also have different curvatures, both straight and sharply curved, and many structural variations, from rigid to soft. Their length can be anything from just centimeters to hundreds of meters. Even though pipelines have such a wide range of attributes, they all need one thing in common, which is regular inspections so that they keep functioning properly. For this, several pipeline inspection robots have been developed for different applications.

Many inspection robots have been developed for navigating pipelines, including wheel-type robots, walking-type robots, crawler-type robots, screw-driven type robots and robots with other locomotion mechanisms. These robots usually have rigid structures and are powered by electric motors and gear transmission systems, which makes them good for inspecting pipelines with larger diameters. But these designs have some limitations. For example they are not flexible, and this makes it hard for them to adapt to pipelines of different sizes. Downsizing these robots is also very challenging, especially for millimeter-scale pipelines like the ones found in biological systems. Also, their mechanisms are intricate and need complex assembly structures, which need a lot of maintenance and can also fail if debris gets into their joints. Using soft material can reduce these drawbacks by making the robot completely soft.

Soft robots are a promising technology for pipeline inspection. Because they are flexible, they can conform to many different pipeline shapes and sizes, and they can interact safely with the inside of the pipeline, which is especially important for biological pipelines. Most of the existing soft robot designs for pipeline inspection use fluid for locomotion, using a supply of air or hydraulic pressure to generate the motion. These include inchworm-type, earthworm-type and growing-type robots. Their design is relatively simple, so they are a scalable alternative to the rigid robots. But even with these advantages, the fluidic-based designs have common drawbacks, like slower speeds and less durability. The deeper the robots go into the pipeline, the more the fluidic response delays become a problem. They can also rupture, especially in industrial pipelines where there may be debris. So there is a clear need for new solutions that keep the merits of soft robots but address their drawbacks.

We take inspiration from nature and propose an ovipositor-inspired flexible locomotion system (Fig. 1). It uses reciprocating flexible sliders to propel itself, and it adapts to tubes of different shapes and sizes by a mechanical inflation technique. This way it keeps the advantages of the soft structure but does not have the downsides of fluidic-based designs. In this study we turned this principle into a fully functional prototype, and we validated and tested it experimentally. The rest of the paper is organized like this: in Section II we give an overview of the working principle, the detailed design and the prototype development of the locomotion system. In Section III we describe the experiments we did to validate and characterize the prototype. After that we present and discuss the experimental results, and then we give a conclusion and an outlook for the future in Section V.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
INTRODUCTION
Pipelines are a ubiquitous means of transporting fluid media, with a significant impact on many aspects of our daily lives. They fulfill many roles, from the transportation of water, gases, and oils to the circulation of bodily fluids. These pipelines vary widely in size, from sub-millimeter dimensions within biological systems to industrial pipelines measuring tens of centimeters. They also have diverse curvatures, both straight and sharply curved, and a wide range of structural variations, from rigid to soft. Their length can range from mere centimeters to hundreds of meters. Despite this wide range of attributes, all pipelines share one common need: regular inspections to ensure that they function properly. For this purpose, several pipeline inspection robots have been developed for different applications.

Various inspection robots have been developed for pipeline navigation, including wheel-type [1,2], walking-type [3], crawler-type robots [4], screw-driven type [5] and other locomotion mechanisms [6,7]. These robots usually have rigid structures powered by electric motors and gear transmission systems, which makes them well-suited for inspecting pipelines with larger diameters. However, these designs have certain limitations, such as a lack of flexibility that limits their adaptability to pipelines of different sizes. Downsizing these robots poses significant challenges, particularly for millimeter-scale pipelines as found in biological systems. Furthermore, their intricate mechanisms require complex assembly structures, which are maintenance-intensive and also prone to failure if debris enters their joints. Using soft material can alleviate these drawbacks by making the robot completely soft.

Soft robots have emerged as a promising technology for pipeline inspection. Their intrinsic flexibility lets them conform to a variety of pipeline shapes and sizes and ensures safe interaction with pipeline interiors, which is particularly crucial for biological pipelines. Most existing soft robotic designs for pipeline inspection rely on fluid for locomotion, using a supply of air or hydraulic pressure to generate the motion, including inchworm-type [9,10,11], earthworm-type [12,13] and growing-type [14] robots. Their relatively simple design offers a scalable alternative to rigid robots. Despite these advantages, fluidic-based designs share common drawbacks such as slower speeds and reduced durability. As the robots go deeper into pipelines, fluidic response delays become more pronounced. In addition, they are susceptible to rupture, especially in industrial pipelines where debris may be present. Hence, there is a clear need for novel solutions that retain the merits of soft robots while addressing their drawbacks.

Inspired by nature, we propose an ovipositor-inspired flexible locomotion system, Fig. 1, that uses reciprocating flexible sliders to propel itself while adapting to tubes of different shapes and sizes through a mechanical inflation technique, keeping the advantages of the soft structure while eliminating the downsides of fluidic-based designs. In this study, we translated this principle into a fully functional prototype, which we validated and tested experimentally. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: in Section II, we give an overview of the working principle, detailed design and prototype development of the proposed locomotion system. In Section III, we describe the experiments conducted to validate and characterize the developed prototype. We then present and discuss the experimental results, followed by a conclusion and outlook for the future in Section V.
